The present invention relates to methods and systems for bi-planar fluoroscopy, such as with dual fluoroscopes mounted to C-arms for lateral and anterior-posterior (AP) fluoroscopy of a patient. In one aspect of the invention, a bi-planar fluoroscopy system may generally include first and second fluoroscopes. In general, each fluoroscope may be positioned and aimed to provide different viewing angles and/or orientations of the target, such as, for example, placement for lateral and AP views of the target. In some exemplary embodiments, both fluoroscopes may be maintained as “fixed or locked” in AP and lateral positions, respectively, for example, and then each controlled by a set of proximally located control mechanisms, such as one control mechanism (e.g. a foot pedal or voice command specific to operation of a given fluoroscope each). The control mechanisms may further be adapted for use by a single operator individually and/or simultaneously. This may be particularly desirable for spinal procedures, such as for pedicle screw or kyphoplasty balloon placement, and may provide significantly enhanced efficiency and time reduction for these procedures, by completely negating subsequent movements after initial AP and lateral positions have been fixed with C-arms locked into such positions.

outputs.L1:
The present invention relates to methods and systems for biplanar fluoroscopy, such as systems employing dual fluoroscopes mounted on C-arms to provide lateral and anterior-posterior (AP) fluoroscopic views of a patient. In one aspect, a biplanar fluoroscopy system may generally include first and second fluoroscopes. Each fluoroscope may be positioned and oriented to provide a different viewing angle and/or orientation of a target, such as lateral and AP views of the target.

In certain exemplary embodiments, the fluoroscopes may be maintained in “fixed or locked” AP and lateral positions, respectively, and controlled by proximally located control mechanisms. For example, each fluoroscope may be operated by a dedicated control mechanism, such as a foot pedal or fluoroscope-specific voice command. The control mechanisms may further be configured for individual and/or simultaneous use by a single operator.

Such a system may be particularly advantageous for spinal procedures, including pedicle screw placement or kyphoplasty balloon placement. By eliminating the need for subsequent movement after the initial AP and lateral positions have been established and the C-arms locked in place, the system may significantly improve procedural efficiency and reduce procedure time.
outputs.L2:
The invention concerns techniques and equipment for bi-planar fluoroscopic imaging, including configurations in which two fluoroscopes are mounted on C-arms to obtain lateral and anterior-posterior (AP) images of a patient. In one implementation, the system generally comprises a first fluoroscope and a second fluoroscope. The two devices may be arranged and directed to capture the target from distinct angles or orientations—for instance, one providing a lateral view and the other an AP view.

In certain exemplary configurations, the fluoroscopes may remain fixed or locked in their respective AP and lateral positions. Each device can then be operated through a nearby, dedicated control, such as a separate foot pedal or fluoroscope-specific voice command. These controls may allow one operator to activate the fluoroscopes either independently or at the same time. Such an arrangement may be especially useful during spinal interventions, including pedicle-screw insertion and kyphoplasty-balloon placement. By locking the C-arms in the desired AP and lateral orientations at the outset and eliminating the need for later repositioning, the system may substantially improve procedural efficiency and reduce operating time.
outputs.L3:
The invention provides methods and systems for bi-planar fluoroscopy using two fluoroscopes, such as fluoroscopic imaging devices mounted on separate C-arms. The fluoroscopes are positioned at different viewing angles relative to a target anatomical region, typically to provide complementary lateral and anterior-posterior views.

Once properly aligned, each fluoroscope may be fixed and locked in position, eliminating the need for repeated repositioning during a procedure. A single operator can control the fluoroscopes either independently or simultaneously through conveniently located controls, such as foot pedals, voice-activated commands, or other proximal control interfaces.

By providing concurrent or readily selectable imaging from two different planes, the system may streamline image-guided procedures and reduce overall procedure time. This approach may be particularly beneficial in spinal interventions, including the placement of pedicle screws and kyphoplasty balloons, where accurate visualization from multiple angles is important.
outputs.L4:
A bi-planar fluoroscopy system incorporates two fluoroscopes mounted on separate C-arms and positioned at different orientations relative to the patient. For example, one fluoroscope may be aligned to provide an anteroposterior (AP) view, while the second provides a lateral view. Once the desired imaging planes have been established, both fluoroscopes remain fixed in position throughout the relevant portion of the procedure. Each unit may be operated independently or both may be activated in coordinated or simultaneous fashion by a single user through readily accessible controls, such as foot pedals, hand controls, or voice-activated commands.

This configuration enables the clinician to obtain images from two complementary perspectives without repeatedly rotating, translating, or otherwise repositioning a single fluoroscope. It can therefore reduce interruptions associated with equipment movement, image-plane realignment, and confirmation of anatomical landmarks. Maintaining fixed AP and lateral views may also improve consistency between successive images and allow the operator to monitor the position, trajectory, and depth of instruments or implants more efficiently.

The system is particularly useful during image-guided spinal interventions. During pedicle screw placement, for example, the AP view can assist with mediolateral alignment and identification of the pedicle, while the lateral view can help assess instrument depth and cephalocaudal trajectory. Similarly, during kyphoplasty, the two views can facilitate advancement of access instruments and positioning of an inflatable bone tamp or balloon within the vertebral body. Because both perspectives are available without moving the imaging equipment after initial alignment, the system can streamline workflow, shorten procedure time, and reduce the physical and logistical demands placed on the clinical team. Appropriate imaging protocols and radiation-safety measures remain necessary to limit exposure to the patient and operating-room personnel.
outputs.L5:
**The Power of “The” and “This”**

“The” and “this” are small words with important roles in English. “The” identifies a specific person, place, object, or idea already known to the reader. “This” points to something particular that is close, current, or especially relevant.

Together, these words make communication clearer. Consider the sentence, “This is the solution to the problem.” Here, “this” draws attention to a specific solution, while “the” indicates a particular problem. Although simple, both words help connect ideas and guide the reader’s focus.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a patent-style summary describing a bi-planar fluoroscopy system with two C-arm fluoroscopes fixed in AP and lateral positions and independently controlled by one operator.
counterfactuals.output:
## Summary

Disclosed is a bi-planar fluoroscopy system configured to provide substantially orthogonal radiographic views of a subject. The system includes a first C-arm fluoroscope positioned in an anterior-posterior (AP) orientation and a second C-arm fluoroscope positioned in a lateral orientation. The C-arm fluoroscopes are supported in fixed operative positions relative to a patient support, thereby permitting acquisition of AP and lateral fluoroscopic images without repositioning either fluoroscope during a procedure.

A common operator control station is communicatively coupled to both fluoroscopes and enables a single operator to control the first and second fluoroscopes independently. The control station may include one or more hand controls, foot controls, touch-screen interfaces, or combinations thereof for selectively initiating image acquisition, adjusting exposure parameters, selecting imaging modes, and controlling image display for either fluoroscope. The system may permit activation of the fluoroscopes individually, alternately, sequentially, or, where permitted, concurrently.

Images acquired by the respective fluoroscopes may be presented on separate displays or in designated regions of a common display, with each image identified according to its AP or lateral orientation. A control processor may coordinate image acquisition, storage, synchronization, dose monitoring, and retrieval while maintaining independent imaging settings for each fluoroscope. Safety interlocks may prevent unintended simultaneous exposure, limit radiation output, and provide visual or audible indications identifying the active imaging plane. The disclosed arrangement facilitates efficient acquisition of orthogonal fluoroscopic views while reducing equipment repositioning and enabling operation of both imaging planes by one operator.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an “aspect of the invention” section for a dual-fluoroscope imaging system designed to improve efficiency during spinal procedures such as pedicle screw and kyphoplasty balloon placement.
counterfactuals.output:
## Aspects of the Invention

In one aspect, the invention provides a dual-fluoroscope imaging system configured to facilitate image-guided spinal procedures. The system comprises a first fluoroscope positioned to acquire images of a target spinal region from a first imaging orientation and a second fluoroscope positioned to acquire images of the target spinal region from a second imaging orientation different from the first imaging orientation. For example, the first and second fluoroscopes may be arranged to obtain substantially anteroposterior and lateral views, respectively, without requiring repeated repositioning of a single fluoroscope.

In another aspect, the first and second fluoroscopes are supported by independently movable positioning assemblies. A controller may coordinate movement of the positioning assemblies to establish, maintain, or restore selected imaging geometries relative to a patient support, an operative table, a vertebral level, or an instrument trajectory. The system may store one or more predetermined positions and may return either fluoroscope to a stored position during a procedure.

In another aspect, the system includes a registration subsystem configured to determine a spatial relationship between the first fluoroscope, the second fluoroscope, the patient, and/or one or more surgical instruments. Registration may be performed using radiopaque fiducials, optical markers, electromagnetic sensors, table-position data, image-based anatomical features, or combinations thereof. Images from the fluoroscopes may be calibrated, spatially correlated, and displayed concurrently to provide complementary views of an operative site.

In another aspect, the system includes a display interface that presents images from the first and second fluoroscopes simultaneously or in rapid alternation. The display interface may present live images, last-image-hold images, stored reference images, or combinations thereof. Corresponding anatomical landmarks, instrument locations, planned trajectories, depth indicators, vertebral labels, or safety boundaries may be overlaid on one or both image sets.

In another aspect, the system is configured to assist placement of a pedicle screw. A planned screw trajectory may be defined using images acquired from one or both fluoroscopes, and the system may display the position and orientation of an access needle, guidewire, drill, tap, or screw relative to the planned trajectory. The two imaging orientations may permit assessment of mediolateral alignment and insertion depth without moving a single fluoroscope between anteroposterior and lateral positions.

In another aspect, the system is configured to assist a vertebral augmentation procedure, including kyphoplasty. Images from the two fluoroscopes may be used to monitor advancement of an access cannula, placement and expansion of a balloon tamp, restoration of vertebral height, and/or delivery of bone cement. Substantially concurrent imaging from different orientations may improve visualization of balloon position, cement distribution, and potential migration beyond a selected treatment region.

In another aspect, image acquisition by the first and second fluoroscopes is synchronized or interleaved. The controller may prevent simultaneous x-ray emission, reduce cross-scatter, coordinate detector readout, or select acquisition timing based on instrument movement, respiration, user input, or a procedural step. The system may automatically select pulse rate, exposure level, collimation, magnification, or field of view independently for each fluoroscope.

In another aspect, the system includes collision-avoidance functionality. Position sensors and a controller may identify a potential collision between the fluoroscopes, the patient, the operative table, personnel, or other equipment. In response, the controller may inhibit movement, limit a movement range, provide an alert, or generate an alternative movement path while preserving a desired imaging orientation.

In another aspect, the system provides a coordinated control interface through which an operator may control both fluoroscopes. The interface may include a foot control, hand control, touchscreen, voice interface, sterile control device, or combinations thereof. A single operator command may initiate image acquisition from both orientations, switch between fluoroscopes, store paired images, recall a positioning preset, or adjust imaging parameters.

In another aspect, the system is configured to reduce procedural interruptions associated with repositioning imaging equipment. By maintaining two fluoroscopes at different imaging orientations, the system may reduce the number of C-arm movements, personnel repositioning steps, image reacquisitions, and associated workflow delays during spinal instrumentation or vertebral augmentation.

In another aspect, the system includes radiation-management features. The controller may track cumulative exposure separately for each fluoroscope, estimate patient or operator dose, recommend or impose acquisition limits, vary imaging parameters according to the selected view, and display dose-related information. The system may preferentially use a stored image from one orientation while acquiring a live image from the other orientation.

In another aspect, the system records paired or time-correlated images together with fluoroscope position, imaging parameters, instrument information, and procedural events. The recorded information may be used for documentation, quality review, navigation, or subsequent confirmation of implant or treatment-device placement.

In another aspect, a method of performing an image-guided spinal procedure comprises positioning a first fluoroscope to image a spinal target from a first orientation, positioning a second fluoroscope to image the spinal target from a second orientation, acquiring images from the first and second fluoroscopes without repositioning either fluoroscope between the orientations, displaying the acquired images, and advancing a surgical instrument based at least in part on information shown in both images. The method may further comprise registering the images, defining a planned trajectory, monitoring insertion depth, detecting deviation from the planned trajectory, and providing an alert or guidance indication.

In another aspect, the first and second imaging orientations need not be exactly orthogonal. The orientations may be selected according to patient anatomy, vertebral level, operative approach, table configuration, or instrument trajectory and may include anteroposterior, lateral, oblique, cranial-caudal, or other projections.

The foregoing aspects may be implemented individually or in any suitable combination. References to particular spinal procedures, imaging orientations, controls, and positioning arrangements are illustrative and do not limit the invention to the expressly described embodiments.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe a medical imaging invention that uses locked anterior-posterior and lateral fluoroscopes, each activated by a dedicated foot pedal or voice command.
counterfactuals.output:
### Dual-Plane, Independently Triggered Fluoroscopy System

The invention is a medical imaging system comprising two fluoroscopes positioned in fixed, orthogonal orientations:

- an **anterior–posterior (AP) fluoroscope**, aligned to produce frontal images; and  
- a **lateral fluoroscope**, aligned to produce side-view images.

Once positioned relative to the patient and operating table, each fluoroscope is mechanically locked to preserve image registration throughout a procedure. The fluoroscopes are independently activated: a dedicated foot pedal or recognized voice command initiates imaging from the corresponding AP or lateral unit. Distinct pedal geometry, labels, or voice confirmations help prevent selection errors.

A controller coordinates exposure timing, displays the selected projection, records dose data, and may prevent unintended simultaneous irradiation. Safety features can include pedal guards, command confirmation, audible or visual exposure indicators, emergency shutoff, collision detection, and configurable pulse-rate and dose limits.

The arrangement allows a clinician to obtain either orthogonal view without moving the imaging equipment or relying on an assistant, supporting rapid, reproducible imaging during procedures such as fracture fixation, spinal instrumentation, catheter placement, and other image-guided interventions.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a formal patent specification paragraph for a system allowing a single clinician to control two fixed C-arm fluoroscopes individually or simultaneously without repositioning them during surgery.
counterfactuals.output: A surgical imaging system comprises a first fixed C-arm fluoroscope and a second fixed C-arm fluoroscope positioned relative to an operative field, and a clinician-operated control interface communicatively coupled to respective control units of the first and second fluoroscopes. The control interface is configured to receive a selection input identifying the first fluoroscope, the second fluoroscope, or both fluoroscopes, and to responsively enable a single clinician to initiate, terminate, and adjust fluoroscopic image acquisition by the selected fluoroscope or fluoroscopes independently or substantially simultaneously. The system may synchronize imaging parameters, including exposure timing, pulse rate, radiation dose, collimation, image orientation, and image-display routing, while permitting separate parameter settings for each fluoroscope. The first and second fluoroscopes are maintained in respective predetermined fixed positions during a surgical procedure such that images from different viewing orientations are selectively acquired without physically repositioning either fluoroscope, thereby reducing workflow interruptions and enabling coordinated multi-view visualization of the operative field.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain, in patent language, how bi-planar fluoroscopy can reduce procedure time by maintaining two fluoroscopes at different viewing angles and using proximally located controls.
counterfactuals.output:
In one embodiment, a bi-planar fluoroscopic imaging system includes first and second fluoroscopes maintained at respective, different viewing angles relative to a procedural region. The fluoroscopes may thereby acquire substantially simultaneous or selectively alternating images along two distinct imaging planes, such as anteroposterior and lateral planes, without requiring repeated repositioning of a single fluoroscope. Maintaining the fluoroscopes at the respective viewing angles reduces equipment movement, image reacquisition, and associated interruptions during instrument navigation, implant placement, or anatomical verification.

The system may further include one or more proximally located controls positioned within reach of an operator adjacent to the patient or sterile field. The controls may permit the operator to activate either fluoroscope, select an imaging plane, initiate image acquisition, adjust imaging parameters, or display acquired images without moving to a remotely located console. Accordingly, the combination of maintained bi-planar viewing angles and proximally accessible controls reduces procedural workflow steps and operator movement and may thereby decrease overall procedure time while facilitating continuous visualization of the procedural region.
